en: Now not one of those signs appeared.
What is here today is gone tomorrow;
One day it shows its back,
Another day its face—
Such is this worthless world!
When the enemy came in a flood,
And the signs of battle appeared,
The black-mottled leopard
Would spring up from beneath him,
Carry word to the enemy,
And go forth fully roused.
The stunted gray wolf-lion
Would seem ready to rend anything he reached,
Ready to unleash calamity,
And would lunge wildly about.
Now not one of those signs appeared.
Despairing of his borrowed life,
His breast burned and his heart was an ember.
The mighty black bird Zymyruk,
Whenever it saw the opposing foe
And gave its rumbling cry,
Whenever the war drum sounded once,
That mighty black bird Zymyruk
Would seem ready to seize the enemy at once,
Thrusting its taloned feet out before him.
On seeing this sign,
The enemy would panic, lose their senses,
And flee without facing him.
Now not one of those signs appeared.
Damn this deceiver—
This worthless world has betrayed me!
The white male camel with a black head
Would appear ready to kneel and crush all beneath it;
When it faced a hostile foe,
It would rear and lunge wildly.
Now the eye could see nothing;
No one knew where
The sacred power had gone.
Such a deceiver is this world—
No one can tell what it truly is.
He climbed the ridge and gazed ahead;
Seeing no sign, his heart burned.
Swaying as though struck from this side,
The lion Semetey stood there.
May God never show us such a sight!
Before anyone could say a word,
In the blink of an eye,
A pale-gray banner rose,
And an ever-mounting uproar broke out.
They had the look of Kyrgyz,
And when they joined battle,
A fury that simply overwhelmed all.
Their white standard became their banner,
Their white-and-mottled pennant fluttered.
A roar split the heavens,
Their war cries deafened the ears,
Dust flew into the sky,
The army seethed amid clouds of dust,
Dividing into many formations,
The vast host spread out in splendor,
Appearing like ravening beasts,
A blue haze flooded the land,
The earth was covered by spear-bearing men,
Too many for the eye to encompass,
Like tumbleweed driven by the wind,
Their identity could not be discerned,
Countless surging troops roared.
When they listened to the tumult,
When they learned what the uproar meant,
Ahead there was shouting,
The people surged and the host clamored,
Crying “Kyyaz!” as their battle cry,
Sword tips flashed separately,
Spears appeared as thick as fish bones.
It seemed they had been roused to frenzy—
The countless host of Kyyaz
Of the Jediger, bending the earth.
In a myriad-strong army no one stands apart;
Among those countless troops brought forth,
What kinds were there, and what kinds were not?
Within those forces,
When a black musket cracked,
Some would flee until they died;
When a short musket snapped,
Some would start and fall from their horses.
Some would behold the enemy’s courage,
Cry, “Hero, we submit!”
And dismount to surrender.
Their eyes bulging and blazing,
Speechless while misery boiled within,
There were many who merely watched;
There were even more who, at a shout,
Fell from their horses and died.
“Take my horse and coat as spoil—
Only let me live!” they would say,
Clambering stiffly down from the saddle,
Standing helpless once captured;
There were many who surrendered so.
Among the Jediger’s vast host
There were also cowards
Who dared not step outdoors at night;
There were also bunglers
Who swung their battle-axes wide;
When a spear was thrust, they cried out—
There were also men quick to panic;
And if they found the chance,
There were also men who fled to their villages.
There were loud, blustering braggarts,
Swaggerers among them too;
There were also mighty wrestlers,
Most skillful in the stratagems of war;
There were also men who plunged
All who approached into disaster;
Untroubled by the prospect of death,
Looking neither up nor down,
Never thinking they might die,
There were also men who came alongside
And seized foes by the collar;
And there were men who cast others
Into dreadful calamity.
The renowned stood at the front,
The heroes guarded the flanks,
The whip-bearers were at the front,
The courageous guarded the flanks.
Nearly ten thousand spread like a lake,
Not a few, but a multitude,
Firing heavy guns and drawing bows,
Again engulfing all in clamor,
In a din that split the sky.
They brandished blue-steel spears,
Raising their deep-socketed lances
High and crossing them,
And began the great clash.
The renowned rode at the front,
Spurring their bay horses,
While valiant Kyyaz guarded the flank.
Never one to stand idle,
Kadyrbay and Tölöbay
Were the men who bore the standards.
A hero comes, a strong man comes,
The lion named Tölöbay comes;
Yet Kadyrbay’s vast host
Recoils and scatters in terror.
The great host loomed like mist—
The brave hero Semetey
Saw this road filled from every side.
“We marched out against the Khagan’s realm,
O dark, fierce, tireless warriors,
And brought a mighty turmoil upon ourselves.
Having escaped death among the Chinese,
Are we now to die among the Kyrgyz?
Having escaped death at an enemy’s hands,
Are we now to die at our own people’s hands?
Having escaped death through ordinary horses,
Are we now to die through noble steeds?
Having escaped death at an enemy’s hands,
Are we now to die at our kinsmen’s hands?”
Semetey stood there towering.
The mighty Külchoro
Laughed beside him, swelling with courage.
Besides Külchoro and Semetey,
There was not another man with them:
The Jediger were myriad, the hero alone—
Such a wretched thing is this world.
There was no noble steed ready to mount;
When a dear life was hard-pressed,
There was no kinsman to shield it,
No forest into which to flee for cover,
No Nogoy people to give protection.
Alone as a solitary pine,
The grim hero stood alone against many foes—
Such is the loneliness of one without a lord.
Neither Sarykan nor Khan Bakay was there,
Nor any of the dear Kyrgyz
Who once stood as his support.
The calamitous campaign and great turmoil
Had now come upon him;
Surrounding the grim hero from every side,
The vast dark host of Jediger
Was coming to seize him,
Climbing over the forked ridge
And appearing above the pass.
The troops below the grim hero
Raised a clamor and commotion,
Thrusting their spears with menace,
Stirring strife for all to see;
They were climbing across Keng-Kol,
The ground of the great conflict,
And coming to crush
The great and fearsome hero himself.
They swarmed like ants,
Seething and writhing like worms,
Raising the cry of “Jediger!”
Carrying banners enough to bend the earth,
The army seethed and filled the plain,
Not a few, but a multitude.
The renowned rode at the front,
Galloping upon their bay horses,
While dear Kyyaz guarded the flank.
He wore armor no bullet could pierce,
And rode a horse no bullet could overtake.
He had tied up with a snap
The silken tail of his racer, Tootoru.
Kyyaz, hero of the Jediger,
Was both a warrior and a valiant man,
A champion unlike other mortals,
A renowned dark-gray stalwart.
The beloved land of the Seven Valleys
He had conquered through valor and made his domain;
The Jediger of the Seven Rivers
He had settled wherever he reached.
His right shoulder was broad,
He was a hero who could shatter the Oirats;
His left shoulder was broad,
He was a warrior well prepared for battle.
Kyyaz, son of Bagysh,
Was blessed with perfect fortune.
Had his nature been known from the start,
He was a son who would obey
Without arguing against what he was told,
A son destined from the first
To exact the blood-price for his elder brother Toltoy.
Broad-chested and wide-breasted,
Ah, what an imposing fellow he was;
With wide mouth and jutting brow,
Dark in complexion and sharp of eye,
His speech was sharper than that of most men.
Thick-wristed and stone-hearted,
He was powerfully built and fierce.
Such was Kyyaz’s nature:
His stature was like a lofty hill,
And he was a towering man;
Like the broad valley itself,
He stood leaning proudly back.
He had the gaze of a hunting eagle,
The chest of a white lion;
Dust rose from his stride,
And life fled at his angry rumble.
Thick through the body, low in stature,
His whole frame seemed cast from stone;
He was practiced against foes face-to-face—
At the sight of his majesty, flee far away.
The people assembled and the nation stirred;
Ninety beasts were slaughtered at his feast,
And he was given the name Kyyaz.
Having received the elders’ blessing,
He became known as Kyyaz the Hero,
A consummate giant in his own land.
Where the Jediger thronged across the earth,
He became lord of the Jediger,
A stronghold and shelter to his clan,
And over all those people
He became the greatest khan.
His word became law;
Among the Jediger of the Seven Valleys,
He became their prince.
